When King Gojong moved Crown Prince Sado's memorial tablet to Jongmyo, it lost its function as a shrine. reviews.author: Cloud Ywing
reviews.text:
Hamchunwon is a garden from the Joseon Dynasty where the current Seoul National University College of Medicine hospital is located.

In 『Donggukyeojibigo』, the name of the palace garden on the east side of Changgyeonggung Palace and south of Gaeyangmun Gate of Gyeonghuigung Palace is recorded as Hamchunwon, but the most representative one in terms of location and size is the one on the east side of Changgyeonggung Palace.

Hamchunwon began with the construction of Changgyeonggung Palace in the 15th year of King Seongjong (1484), planting trees here and surrounding the fence according to Feng Shui theory, and prohibiting the entry of unrelated people. It was officially named in the 24th year of King Seongjong (1493) and became a garden attached to Changgyeonggung Palace.

During the reign of Yeonsangun, the people's houses outside Hamchunwon were demolished and expanded, the military was deployed, the public was prohibited from passing through, and a gate was built. After that, King Jungjong made the people come back and live again. During the Japanese invasions of Korea, management gradually became neglected, such as temporarily burying Deokbin's body, and during the reign of King Injo, half of Hamchunwon was distributed to Taeboksa Temple. For the next 140 years, it was used as a place to raise horses.

In the 40th year of King Yeongjo's reign (1764), the shrine of Crown Prince Sado was moved here, and when King Jeongjo ascended the throne, this place was called Gyeongmo Palace, and in the 9th year of King Jeongjo's reign (1785), the area was renovated. In the 3rd year of Gwangmu (1899), the memorial tablet of Crown Prince Sado from Gyeongmo Palace was moved to Jongmyo, and Gyeongmo Palace lost its function, and Gyeongmo Palace was renamed Gyeongmojeon. In the 4th year of Gwangmu (1900), Yeonghui-jeon, which enshrined portraits of the six kings, namely Taejo, Sejo, Seongjong, Sukjong, Yeongjo, and Sunjo, was moved and built on the site of Gyeongmo Palace.

Afterwards, after the Japanese colonial rule of the country, Gyeongseong Imperial University was built in the area of ​​Gyeongmo Palace, and most of its original appearance was lost. Due to the Korean War, the old building was burned, making it impossible to see its original appearance.

Hamchunwon is one of the sophisticated buildings of the late Joseon Dynasty, and the only remaining ruins are Hamchunmun Gate.

※The name has been changed to (Hamchunwonji → Seoul Gyeongmogungji).
(Notice on July 28, 2011)
Source: National Cultural Heritage Portal

reviews.author: Youngmin Kim (withpipes)
reviews.text:
Seoul Tangible Cultural Heritage
This building was built in 1868 (the 5th year of King Gojong's reign) as the office building when Heungseon Daewongun revived the Three Military Departments, which were abolished during the reign of King Sejong, in 1865 (the 2nd year of King Gojong's reign). It was the central building among the offices of the three military departments (Cheongheondang, General Affairs Hall, and Deoguidang) established in the late Joseon Dynasty, and was moved to its current location in the 1930s.
At the time, when it was used as the three military departments that commanded the military and took charge of affairs related to the border, the small Cheongheondang and Deokui-dang were located on the left and right, centered around the General Affairs Hall, which was the government office, and were connected by a corridor connecting the two buildings.
However, there is a record that 79 buildings of the government building were destroyed by a fire that occurred in April 1870 (it is unclear whether the General Affairs Hall was rebuilt at the time as it suffered a fire), and that it was rebuilt in October of the same year.
After the three military departments were abolished in 1880, it was used as the Tonggimuamun Gate, the government office that oversaw politics and military affairs in the late Joseon Dynasty, and as a protest building, and during the Japanese colonial period, it was used as the Joseon Infantry Headquarters Building.

On November 5, 2003, Honggyu Choi, who had run a hardware store for over 20 years, opened the store. It was established to collect, preserve, and study Korea's disappearing old locks, and to publicize the beauty and scientific excellence of locks through exhibition activities. About 300 of the 3,000 locks owned by Choi Hong-gyu from Korea and around the world are on display. Soetdae is a dialect word for key.

The 230㎡ museum is located on the 4th floor of a 4-story building and consists of 3 exhibition rooms and an event hall. In the first exhibition room, various locks are displayed by period and shape. There are about 40 locks used in the Joseon Dynasty, including U-shaped locks, round cylindrical locks, box-shaped locks, fish-shaped locks, dragon-shaped locks, and turtle-shaped locks, as well as 3 locks from the Goryeo Dynasty, 1 lock from the Unified Silla Dynasty, 11 bolts, 8 key plates, and 7 large locks.

The second exhibition room displays 15 different types of locks used on wooden furniture of the Joseon Dynasty, including chests, chests, seal boxes, portrait boxes, and raincoats. The third exhibition room displays locks from around the world, including Africa, Europe, Tibet, the Middle East, India, and China. In the fall of 2004, a special exhibition, Blacksmith, was held.

The steel building with a unique exterior, covered on all sides with rusty iron plates, is the work of architect Seung Hyo-sang, and the building's blueprint and model are housed in the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art. On the third floor, there is a gallery space where various cultural events such as art exhibitions, cultural performances, and events are held.

reviews.text:
There is no change in my inability to fathom the bitter feelings I felt while writing this. I am strongly protesting against Google's selective treatment of not posting posts without any reason so that third parties cannot see them. I am writing this post with the determination to not post any more posts on Google if Google's actions continue after seeing whether these posts are also selectively blocked from being viewed by third parties.

Early February. It was a Saturday afternoon when the cold had not yet subsided. I went on a tour around the Naksan Fortress Wall with three or four friends from my hometown. After looking around Heunginjimun, Dongdaemun, and Chi, we begin exploring the trail around Naktasan Mountain (sometimes called Naksan for short), which corresponds to the Left Blue Dragon of Hanyang City Wall. To gain prior knowledge before exploring the Dulle-gil trail, I referred to Hong Sun-min's 'Reading Hanyang City' (Nulwa Publishing Company) and carefully read Yoo Hong-jun's 'My Cultural Heritage Expedition' (Changbi Publishing Company) before setting out on the trail, but there are many things that are lacking.

When Taejo Lee Seong-gye decided to make Hanyang the capital city, he set Baekaksan Mountain as his main mountain and located Gyeongbokgung Palace in front of Baekaksan Mountain as the main palace. Then, he built a city wall that connected Naksan, which corresponds to the left Cheongryong, Mokmyeoksan (Namsan), which corresponds to the main dragon, and Inwangsan, which corresponds to the right Baekho, and then leads back to Baekaksan Mountain. In order to complete a ruling country, it cannot be said that it consists of only a palace and a capital. Jongmyo and Sajik were needed to serve as the governing ideology and spiritual pillars of Joseon. Jongmyo was located in the position of the left blue dragon and Sajik was located in the position of the right Baekho. Only then was a complete nation born.

The Naksan City Wall Exploration Trail plans to tour the city wall that runs above the Naksan Ridge, which corresponds to the Left Blue Dragon. The Naksan City Wall Trail, which starts from Dongdaemun, has a trail outside the castle wall and a trail inside the city wall, so you can feel the charm of each trail in its own way. Whether you choose the inner road or the outer road, if you feel a bit bored while exploring, you can change between the inner and outer roads by using the passages that connect the inside and outside of the castle here and there.

The mountain ridge road has a gentle slope, so you can reach the top without much effort. If you look closely at the walls while moving, you can see at a glance the history of the city's construction from the long 500-year reign of Joseon and the Japanese colonial period to modern times. There is a clear contrast between the construction technology and stone materials of the walls built during the reign of King Taejo Lee Seong-gye, the founding of the Joseon Dynasty (it is said that a significant portion of the walls were made of earthen stone during the reign of King Taejo in order to build the capital as quickly as possible) and the stone materials built during the reign of Sejong, when the foundation of the nation was in place to some extent.Afterwards, during the reigns of various kings, the city wall was continuously repaired or repaired, but the most notable and large-scale repair work was during the reign of King Gwanghaegun due to the Japanese invasions of Korea. After that, there was no recordable repair work. It can be seen from the walls that large-scale repair work was done during the reign of Sukjong. The last large-scale repair work was done during the reign of King Sunjo. The stone materials used in the castle repair work during the reign of Sukjong and Sunjo are The traces of repairs using large, almost square granite are so noticeable that you can immediately notice them.

However, the important fact is that there are almost no records of repairs to the capital from the time of Gwanghaegun until the reign of Sukjong. This is because of the humiliating surrender conditions of the so-called Samjeondo, which established a military-subject relationship due to the personal government of Hong Taiji (later the name of the country was changed to the Qing Dynasty) during the reign of King Injo. One of the terms of surrender was that no new construction or repairs could be made to the capital or defensive walls. In other words, the act of building or repairing the city wall was considered a hostile act against the Qing Dynasty, so they did not even dare to repair the city wall.

Not only Hyojong, who set the Northern Expedition as his top national goal, but also the Seoin (later Noron faction), the ruling power that virtually ruled Joseon, did not want to conquer the North, so they would have had no reason to go against the wishes of the Qing Dynasty. The walls of the city wall were torn down or neglected during the Japanese colonial period and Korea's industrial modernization, and were restored to their current condition, and the walls of Hanyangdoseong were preserved as a record of history.

As you walk along Naksan City Wall, you will find surprising facts engraved here and there on the walls. The fact is that at the time of the founding of the Joseon Dynasty, a real-name architecture system was implemented while the Hanyangdoseong was being built. According to records, air space had to be mobilized from each region to build the city wall. From a certain section to a certain section, Gyeongsang Province people, from a certain section to a certain section, Honam people, and from a certain section to a certain section, Gwanseo people were assigned to each section to build the wall, and the name of the person responsible for building the wall was engraved on each section.

It is a very surprising fact that in the early Joseon Dynasty, a real-name construction system was implemented that strictly held each person responsible for any shoddy construction in the section he or she was responsible for. It is also confirmed again that this architectural real-name system was applied to the newly built Hwaseong Fortress Wall in Suwon by King Jeongjo. If you get a little tired of walking along the Naksan Fortress Wall, it would be fun to take a break at a coffee shop next to the Doseongan-gil Wall.
